Breaking.title: My approach to EU is pragmatic, says Andy Burnham
Breaking.text:
The prime minister has said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything", as he outlined his agreement with the bloc to MPs.

Andy Burnham told the Commons there was "no fixed destination" on talks to explore closer ties with the European Union, adding it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.

After several former prime ministers urged him to not reopen the Brexit debate, Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" - and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

At a summit on Friday, Burnham agreed a new deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

He also finalised the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU and said both sides will "brainstorm" options for their long-term relationship.

He has previously suggested potential options for the future could include rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership.

However, he has ruled out major changes to the UK-EU relationship before the next general election, saying he will stick to Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.

Speaking in the Commons on Monday, Conservative MP Sir Edward Leigh said the "reset" with the EU is "a prelude to the prime minister's sincere desire to rejoin the EU and have another referendum" and risked leading to another Scottish independence referendum.

Burnham replied to the Gainsborough MP: "It's not a prelude to anything. It's a pragmatic approach and it will continue to be a pragmatic approach.

"If it's in Britain's national interest, I will recommend it to this House. If it is not, then I won't. There is no fixed opinion here. There is no fixed destination.

"Europe could change again in the next year, 18 months, and we'll have to obviously watch how life changes. But where Britain can make progress, surely we should make progress."

The prime minister also told MPs the government's forthcoming 10-year plan for the country will consider the "range of options for our long-term relationship with our largest market" - the EU.

MPs heard the "plan for Britain" will be published next month and the results of the "informal exchanges of ideas" with the EU will be presented around the time of their next joint summit.

To laughter from the opposition benches, Burnham said: "So there will be no banging on about Europe from this side or a running commentary."

The words echoed those used by Conservative former Prime Minister Lord Cameron in 2006.

Burnham went on to say there would be a "calm, constructive and pragmatic consideration of what is in Britain's interests in the long-term", adding "always the British people will be the boss and they will decide what comes next".

Conservative MP Sir Bernard Jenkin asked Burnham to "give a clear and unequivocal statement that it would be unthinkable for any prime minister to try and take the UK back into the EU without a referendum".

Burnham replied to the Harwich and North Essex MP : "Yes, it would be unthinkable."

Speaking for the Opposition, Badenoch said Burnham's EU deal "wasn't really about reducing the cost of living" but instead "committing Britain to becoming a rule taker from Brussels, something he had no mandate to do".

Badenoch also said: "Six former prime ministers, including Tony Blair, are criticising the direction he is taking UK-EU relations. He says the prime ministers who implemented a democratic decision are living in the past.

"The only person living in the past is the man trying to take Britain back to 2015 instead of focusing on the future."

Over the weekend, Baroness May, who spent three years negotiating an EU exit deal, told the BBC she was "aghast" Burnham could be considering rejoining.

She urged him to "accept Brexit and move on".

Rishi Sunak has also warned against reopening the "divisive" debate about rejoining the EU, telling Sky News it would be "a huge distraction for government".

Earlier this month, Boris Johnson, who negotiated the original Brexit deal as prime minister, said it was "madness" for Burnham to make Brexit his "political priority".

He told the Daily Telegraph, external, he believed the public would back Brexit again if Burnham forced another vote on the issue.

His predecessor Lord Cameron, who resigned as prime minister after losing the 2016 Brexit referendum, has also warned against "another-decade long debate about whether we should be in or out".

Meanwhile, former Labour Prime Minister Sir Tony - who was a prominent opponent of leaving the EU - has said the UK should only rejoin the bloc if it reforms and allows more innovation on technology.

Asked about the criticism from his predecessors, Burnham earlier told broadcasters: "They're stuck in the past because they can't face up to the bad deal that they did."

He added: "I'm not a prime minister that's going to be stuck in the past."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey welcomed the new agreements before telling the Commons that a "totally new deal for Britain" is needed now.

Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice labelled it a "terrible" deal, while Green Party MP Ellie Chowns said "bold and brave politics, not baby steps" are needed.

Breaking.title: What strike on Russian ship in Libya says about spread of Ukraine war
Breaking.text:
Anchored in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.

The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi, co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?

The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.

Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes, has called it "a dangerous escalation".

It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.

Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.

Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks – what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" – have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.

The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.

And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.

It's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern".

Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar.

As the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches, this war has already been spreading, notably in other parts of Europe.

On Friday, several Russian projectiles landed well inside Poland's borders, just 60 miles from an Anglo-French exercise of forces intended to be deployed following an eventual ceasefire in Ukraine.

This, said Poland's PM Donald Tusk, was "a deliberate provocation" by Moscow.

It's not the first time Russian munitions have landed inside Poland, and therefore inside Nato territory, but observers have pointed out that Russia's probing of Nato's borders is becoming ever more brazen and some are calling for a firmer response.

But Russia is already heavily sanctioned by the West, with Europe having reduced much – but not all – of its energy imports from Russia, so the options for retaliation are limited, short of military confrontation, which no one wants.

Breaking.title: Don Toliver postpones London O2 arena show after Manchester evacuation
Breaking.text:
US rapper Don Toliver has postponed two shows in London this week, after his concert in Manchester on Sunday was evacuated when an "unknown substance" was released into the crowd.

Toliver was due to play The O2 on Monday and Wembley Arena on Tuesday, but Live Nation said his "stage and production equipment remains in Manchester and cannot be moved in time".

One person was taken to hospital and 89 people showed "symptoms believed to be linked to the exposure" after Sunday's Co-op Live arena show, police said.

Fans described "distressing scenes" with people "choking", "screaming" and "coughing up blood" because of the effects of a substance, which police initially believed to be tear gas.

The Wembley show has been rescheduled to 14 December, while Monday night's O2 gig has been moved to 15 December.

"I'm very sad to sit here and say I have to reschedule The O2 London show to December 15th due to (the) unfortunate incident last night," Don Toliver wrote on Instagram.

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) declared a major incident on Sunday and said 12,000 people were evacuated from the arena.

One woman was taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further assessment and treatment after the incident, which happened at about 22:00 GMT, the force said.

A further 88 people "underwent dry decontamination at the scene and were subsequently accommodated within the Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed", according to GMP.

Leon Douzi said he was right next to where the substance was released, and described someone holding a can and "this gas coming out".

"It just hit me in the throat," he said, adding that it felt like "burning".

There was "a bit of panic", Douzi said: "Everybody was having the same feeling and trying to get out."

Some fans reported eye and respiratory symptoms, according to the North West Ambulance Service.

Hannah Baxter, who went to the concert with her partner, said the first thing she noticed was a burning feeling in her throat.

"[We] were just coughing and coughing... there was a guy next to us who had vomited. There were people with red eyes and... tears everywhere," she told the BBC.

Joey Howe, a football journalist at the gig, told BBC Radio Manchester there was a "horrible smell" and added: "People were coming through in wheelchairs choking – it was really distressing."

Police launched an investigation and are continuing to carry out tests on items at the venue to try to identify the substance. No arrests have been made.

Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said: "Enquiries remain ongoing to establish the nature of the substance, where it came from and any associated risk. Testing will take place throughout the day as the investigation into the cause of this incident progresses.

"We are trying to establish whether any criminality has occurred in relation to this incident."

Some fans complained about security and a lack of searches as people went into the Manchester concert.

Jessica Moult-Boffey, of Wigan, said people were "crying and screaming in pain" as they left the venue, adding she felt "confused on how something like that got into a venue of that size".

Malachi Clarke also claimed security was "not good at all", adding: "They weren't checking bags, to the point where I had to ask them if they needed to check mine."

Co-op Live said on its website there were a range of security measures, and while "some of these are visible, others you won't be able to see".

It said the arena used a "frictionless security screening that detects prohibited items without you needing to empty your pockets".

Figen Murray, the mother of a Manchester Arena attack victim who led the campaign for a new law to prevent terrorist attacks at public venues, said people should feel "assured" about security measures.

"A lot of the big venues use mass screening technology, where you don't even know you've been checked," she told the BBC. They also have staff observing CCTV, security guards and plain-clothed officers on site.

Murray said that while the current technology is "good enough", it needed improvement over the next few years to become "more sophisticated".

Venues are currently focused on keeping out items – such as explosives – that could cause mass casualties, she added.

Breaking.title: Andrew received £750,000 from Turkish millionaire, court told
Breaking.text:
A Turkish millionaire has told the High Court she was misled over a £750,000 payment she made to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor in 2019.

Nebahat Isbilen is alleging her former business adviser, Selman Turk, misappropriated £38m of her assets, including a payment to the then-Duke of York which she believed was for help with her passport.

Turk has rejected the allegations, saying the 81-year-old Isbilen knew the money was actually being paid in the hope that Mountbatten-Windsor could help her husband, a politician who is in prison in Turkey.

Mountbatten-Windsor repaid the £750,000 and is expected to give evidence to the High Court in December. He is not accused of any wrongdoing.

Isbilen's lawyers also told the court on Monday that Turk had instructed a separate £15,000 payment to Mountbatten-Windsor's ex-wife, Sarah Ferguson, purportedly for the former Duchess of York's 60th birthday party in 2019, and an unquantified "wedding gift" payment for their daughter Princess Beatrice.

Isbilen's family founded a major soap and cosmetics firm in Turkey.

But when her husband, Ilhan, a former member of the Turkish parliament, was arrested in 2015, she wanted help moving her assets out of Turkey. Her lawyers said the charges were "politically motivated" and that in 2017 she was facing "political persecution".

She left Turkey for Greece in 2017 and moved to London in 2018.

Simon Colton KC, representing Isbilen, said she met Turk in January 2017 and gave him control of most of her financial assets.

But Turk "deliberately and systematically abused" her trust and transferred the money to companies he owned or controlled, Colton added.

Colton added that Isbilen approved the £750,000 payment to Andrew, but that Turk "lied to her" about its purpose, which was "a further example of his dishonesty".

The court heard that Isbilen had a private dinner with the then Duke and Duchess of York at Turk's flat in December 2019 where she discussed her husband's case.

Turk's lawyers told the court that Isbilen understood and directed the management of her own affairs.

Joshua Hitchens, representing Turk, said in written submissions: "In circumstances where the claimant dined with the duke and duchess and discussed her husband with them, she cannot have believed that the £750,000 was a disguised fee for help with a passport, or with a visa."

The trial before Mr Justice Adam Johnson is due to conclude in March, with a written judgment at a later date.

Breaking.title: Blaina girl Lilly Jones stabbed by 14-year-old boy, murder trial told
Breaking.text:
Warning: This article contains details readers may find distressing

A teenage girl was stabbed "around 55 times" by a 14-year-old boy, a murder trial has been told.

Lilly Jones, from Blaina, in Blaenau Gwent, left home at about 18:30 on 20 June, telling her father she was "popping out for a bit".

Her body was discovered face down in woodland close to Duffryn Park two days later.

A 14-year-old boy, who cannot be named because he is under 18, denies her murder.

He and Lilly shared an interest in Pokémon and were "in some kind of relationship", the court heard.

The boy was dressed in a white short-sleeved shirt and tie as he sat in the dock at Newport Crown Court on Monday.

Anna Pope KC, prosecuting, told the jury a camping knife containing a complete DNA profile had been found in the boy's bedroom drawer.

"It was calculated to be a billion times more likely if this DNA had come from Lilly Jones than if it had come from someone else," she said.

Pope said the boy had not given an explanation as to why Lilly's DNA was on the knife.

She added scratch marks were discovered on the inside of his arm and forensic swabs taken from Lilly's fingernails identified his DNA.

She had been stabbed in the heart, both lungs and an artery in her neck. There were 17 stab wounds to her neck, and knife wounds were found on her face, jaw, chest and bottom.

Lilly's phone has never been found.

Newport Crown Court was told Lilly and the boy became friends in March this year after a chance meeting in the street.

They were captured on CCTV cameras in Blaina and were last seen together at 18:50 as they walked towards a footbridge leading to the park, near to where her body was later found.

At 22:19 that evening, Lilly's family contacted the police to report her missing. It was the day after her 14th birthday.

Police searching for Lilly spoke to the teenager the following day. He told officers he was supposed to meet up with Lilly at the Red Lion pub in Blaina, but she never arrived.

He later told police they had been together for part of the previous night, before they separated. He said he came home after she told him she was going to meet up with someone else.

In a further conversation with police on the day Lilly's body was found, he said she had told him she wanted to show him a disused park, before leaving.

When he was arrested he told police he did not murder Lilly and did not know where her phone was.

The trial heard that, when a phone belonging to the defendant was examined, he was found to have searched for Gwent Police, and similar terms, about 30 times the morning after Lilly disappeared, between 05:49 and 10:02.

Pope added: "The phone also showed that photographs had been taken by someone using [the defendant's] phone, we say that's [the defendant]."

She added it was "of note" that one of the photographs "is looking back towards the scene where we say Lilly's body was later found".

Addressing the jury, Pope said: "We will ask you to consider why it is that [the defendant] would take a photograph of some distance, of the area where we know Lilly to have died that night? Particularly if, as he suggests, he left her alive, when she was going to meet a friend."

The trial continues.

Breaking.title: Gisèle Pelicot 'humiliated' after nude photos sent to media to promote book
Breaking.text:
Gisèle Pelicot has said she has been "once again humiliated" after nude images of her were sent to the media to promote a book about coercive control.

The 73-year-old told French broadcaster BFM TV she would take legal action against the publisher and author of the essay.

Pelicot made headlines across the world when she waived her right to anonymity in the trial of her then-husband Dominique, who was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping her, as well as allowing other men to rape her while she was unconscious.

The publisher apologised, saying it would no longer print or promote the work after "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".

Pelicot told BFM: "I am deeply shocked that images from the most intimate part of my private life are being displayed and exploited for commercial purposes."

"Today I find myself once again humiliated, exposed and hurt, as if the ordeal of the trial had not been enough," she said.

The essay was written by Sabine Prokhoris, a philosopher and psychoanalyst, who has previously criticised the Me Too movement.

French media reported that Tinbad, a small Paris publishing house, emailed nude photos of Pelicot taken by her ex-husband to some media outlets in order to promote the essay.

In a statement on its website, Tinbad said that no further print runs of the book would be produced beyond the 280 copies already in circulation.

"We offer our sincerest apologies to Ms Gisèle Pelicot," it said. The company also apologised to the author.

Tinbad said "no images of rape or pornographic videos" were sent to the media.

French news agency AFP quoted the blurb of the book as saying coercive control was "a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy".

"These psychological situations, fundamentally ambiguous in nature, involve each of the parties in an equally responsible, though not symmetrical, way," it said.

Pelicot's lawyer Christophe Bigot told BFM the book "calls into question her status as a victim".

Prokhoris told AFP that she placed "full responsibility" for the "inappropriate" promotional campaign on her publisher.

Fifty men were convicted alongside Pelicot's ex-husband in 2024, in a case that made her a global feminist icon.

After her husband was arrested for secretly filming underneath women's skirts in a supermarket, she discovered she had been repeatedly raped by dozens of men, including her husband, while unconscious, over a period of nearly a decade.

Pelicot said she decided to waive her right to anonymity to show how "shame has to change sides" from victims to perpetrators.

Breaking.title: Comedian impersonates Trump's dance moves, mocks trade talks at Canada press dinner
Breaking.text:
Prime Minister Mark Carney brought a Donald Trump impersonator on stage at Ottawa's annual press gallery dinner, where he poked fun at strained US-Canada relations and on-again, off-again trade talks.

The impersonator, played by comedian Mark Critch of the sketch comedy show This Hour Has 22 Minutes, came out after Carney jokingly pressed an "emergency comedy button" during his speech.

Critch appeared alongside another actor impersonating Carney, played by Canadian sketch comedian Mark McKinney.

"We've got two Carneys here, it's a disaster," the Trump impersonator said after he walked on stage.

Using some of Trump's signature mannerisms, like his dance moves and his slightly hunched posture, he joked about the latest US midterm elections, which led to Trump's Republican Party losing control in Congress.

"I'm so popular we just had a big BLUE WAVE in the states," the impersonator said at the Saturday press gala.

He also took aim at ongoing US-Canada trade negotiations, saying,"We're going to have a great deal. There's only one thing standing in the way: me, because I'm crazy."

There were also jabs at Trump's search for a new White House press secretary following Katie Zacharia's exit, and at US ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra, who is unpopular among Canadians.

"I said 'find somebody who is less likeable than me,' and we got one," the Trump impersonator joked about Hoekstra.

Carney stood behind him occasionally laughing. The prime minister also delivered his own zingers, saying at one point: "This is a tough room. And I've been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator."

Both Critch and McKinney - the two impersonators - are fixtures of This Hour Has 22 Minutes, a long-standing Canadian sketch comedy show that has recently enjoyed viral internet fame for its timely skits mocking the Trump administration.

The skits, published directly on Tik Tok and YouTube, have depicted Zacharia's quick ouster, external and poked fun at rapper Nicki Minaj's, external support for Trump.

They have garnered millions of views, and even captured the attention of major US media., external

Critch and McKinney's appearance at Saturday's dinner is part of an evening of traditionally light-hearted humour, where Canadian politicians poke fun at one another at a gala hosted by the Canadian Parliamentary Press Gallery.

In a separate speech, Canada's governor general, Louise Arbour, joked about Carney's popularity and frequent global travel.

"Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he's supposed to be," Arbour said.

Breaking.title: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drones in Libya, Zelensky says
Breaking.text:
A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones at a port in Libya on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

There was an explosion on the warship at the Benghazi naval base in the early morning, while it was docking for fuel and supplies ahead of its return to Russia, local authorities said.

Zelensky added that Ukraine's attack hit a second Russian vessel, a cargo ship which he claimed was being used to transport weapons.

The local health ministry said it had received injured people from a commercial ship that was targeted off the coast of the port. It is not clear whether this is the same vessel as the one Ukraine has claimed responsibility for.

Following the strikes, the Kremlin warned of an "escalation of tensions in the region", but declined to comment directly on the attacks in Libya.

Libya's two governments - the UN-recognised government in the capital, Tripoli, and a rival administration in the east - have both condemned the attack.

The Tripoli foreign ministry said the country would not accept being drawn into the conflict.

It said foreign forces would not be allowed to use Libyan ports and civilian infrastructure for military purposes.

The eastern government, based in Benghazi, called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty.

Seven naval drones were deployed to target and sink the corvette Merkury, one of Russia's newest ships, Zelensky said in a statement on Monday. He added that a Ka-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed.

The Ukrainian president said the second ship was the MV ANGARA, a Russian container carrier.

The attack came the day after a Russian cargo vessel was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland. The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning.

Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely to be behind the attack. Kyiv has not commented.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Monday that the "expansion of terrorist activity in the Baltic" was a "dangerous trend" and has said "it is, of course, leading to an escalation of tensions in the region."

When questioned over the attacks in Libya, Peskov said information would be provided by the country's defence ministry and added: "We paid attention to Zelensky's statements about it".

Peskov declined to comment on the strikes on Russian ships in Libya and said that that information would be provided by Russia's Defence Ministry.

The UN mission in Libya expressed "serious concern" over the attacks on Sunday, calling for "an immediate, independent and transparent investigation".

"Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts," the UNSMIL wrote on X., external

Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship that was struck in the morning engulfed in flames and smoke. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC also shows a boat on fire at 05:47 GMT at the Benghazi port.

Breaking.title: What failure of COP31 reveals about a divided world
Breaking.text:
Some may have found it ironic that the world's biggest conference on climate change should collapse over the very mention of fossil fuels - the main cause of global warming.

Yet that is what happened in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday.

The failure tells us something about the state of climate diplomacy. But it may tell us even more about the increasingly divided world in which the negotiations take place.

Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who led the negotiations, spoke of a backdrop constituting "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". The competing demands, he said, had become "unbridgeable red lines".

Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister and the summit's president, was blunter. Governments should not disappoint people desperate for climate action, he suggested, by getting "hung up on one word or phrase".

And Kurum had a point. Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, there was agreement to transition away from fossil fuels. The proposed Antalya Pact failed to mention them at all.

Was it really worth sacrificing the agreement over two words, then?

The countries that rejected it said the distinction was fundamental. They argued that there was a world of difference between promising to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and committing to move away from the fuels responsible for most of them. Without that explicit commitment, they feared the new agreement would weaken the one made in Dubai.

Normally, it is difficult to establish exactly who has said what at these conferences. Much of the bargaining takes place behind closed doors, and governments are often reluctant to admit which proposals they have opposed.

This time, some of the opposition was public - mostly from oil-producing nations.

Mohammad Ayoub, a Saudi negotiator speaking on behalf of the 22 Arab League countries, argued that Arab nations had contributed less than 2% of historical greenhouse gas emissions. It was wealthy industrialised nations, he said, that bore the overwhelming responsibility for the problem.

He defended the Arab countries' right to choose how to tackle climate change according to their national circumstances.

Russia's delegate Sergei Kononuchenko went further. Cutting oil and gas supplies before demand fell, he warned, would cause shortages, higher prices and energy poverty.

"For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel," he said.

The wider political backdrop was still more revealing.

The US, which in previous rounds of talks had helped broker compromises - sometimes working alongside China - had no official delegation in Antalya. President Donald Trump has rejected the entire international climate process.

And while delegates argued over fossil fuels in Turkey, Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen that included a pledge to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products.

The priorities of some of the world's most powerful governments appeared very different from those being discussed in the negotiating rooms.

Yet, perhaps, the picture is more optimistic than it first appears. About 130 governments backed a demand for explicit language on moving away from fossil fuels - roughly two-thirds of the countries represented in Antalya.

Christiana Figueres, who led the UN negotiations that delivered the Paris Agreement, argued that countries were right to walk away rather than endorse a weaker political commitment that might undermine the progress already made.

Looked at this way, the collapse is not evidence that the world has lost its appetite for climate action. Quite the opposite - a substantial majority of governments were demanding more ambitious action.

So why not simply find a way for them to move ahead without waiting for the countries determined to block them?

The difficulty becomes clearer when you look beyond the dispute over fossil fuels.

Kononuchenko had another target in his sights: climate finance. Much of the money wealthy countries provide to poorer nations, he complained, comes as loans rather than grants. He said that developing countries ended up repaying more than they received.

"This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner," he declared.

Then, in a striking moment, he leaned towards the microphone and switched from Russian into English to address his criticism directly to the Europeans: "First of all distinguished representatives of the EU."

Russia has its own reasons for attacking Europe, but the complaint about finance is one that many developing countries share. They argue that they are being asked to pay for damage they did little to cause while receiving too little help to adapt to climate change or build cleaner economies.

The EU had ruled out significant new funding before the negotiations began. Mohamed Adow, the Kenyan campaigner who heads Power Shift Africa, accused Europe of rejecting a flawed deal while refusing to acknowledge its own responsibility for the failure on finance.

Perhaps the most poignant aspect of the failed Antalya Pact is what the countries had apparently been prepared to accept.

The final draft expressed "deep concern" that global warming was expected to exceed 1.5°C in the next few years. It warned that further warming would cause increasingly serious damage, some of it irreversible, and called for urgent action to limit how far temperatures rose above that threshold.

This remarkably strong language had survived into the final version, apparently without provoking the opposition that sank the agreement. Even countries bitterly divided over fossil fuels and finance seemed prepared to acknowledge the scale of the danger.

Yet they couldn't agree on how to respond.

And that, perhaps, is what Antalya tells us about the state of international climate co-operation. The problem isn't simply finding the right words or changing the voting rules. It is persuading countries with very different interests to take action that no international authority can compel them to take.

That was always going to be difficult. In today's divided world, it looks harder than ever.
Breaking.description: Some may have found it ironic that the world's biggest conference on climate change should collapse over the very mention of fossil fuels - the main cause of global warming. Yet that is what happened in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday. The failure tells us something about the state of climate diplomacy. But it may tell...

Breaking.title: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
Breaking.text:
Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the charity Oxfam says, external.

Heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and dioxins and biological contaminants are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.

Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, said the impact on Gaza "will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival".

In response, the Israeli embassy in the UK said the report "falls short of professional standards".

Behar also accused Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza".

Israel has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. It maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.

Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.

The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".

Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials.

"There are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment," Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC.

She says that now and in future Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.

With all six wastewater treatment plants out of operation in Gaza, untreated sewage currently makes its way into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea. The health impact has recently been exacerbated by heavy winter storms causing rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people.

Testing types and levels of contamination is often not possible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and there are Israeli restrictions on the entry of specialist testing equipment and scientists. The BBC has approached the Israeli military for comment.

UNEP said security concerns also prevented its expert staff from previously travelling to Gaza.

The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to be carried out in Gaza to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up. It says special attention must be given to the protection of workers involved.

The Israeli embassy sharply criticised the report, arguing that it relied on satellite imagery "and unverified assumptions, and its methodology lacks the academic rigour needed to withstand serious scrutiny".

It said the report drew conclusions about Gaza's soil and groundwater without considering the excavation of hundreds of kilometres of tunnels by Hamas, rendering it fundamentally flawed.

Farmers and those working in fishing say that pollution of the soil and sea mean they are unable to produce food that is safe.

"Sewage and wastewater are discharged into the sea without treatment and this is a great disaster," complains fisherman Abu al-Abed Sultan. "There is also rubble from destroyed houses that's dumped into the sea. When we lower our nets, we catch rubble and garbage. This harms the marine environment; the fish are affected and so are the fishermen."

At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The UN says that humanitarian conditions remain dire.

Israel has conditioned large-scale Gaza reconstruction on the full disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups. In July, Hamas accepted a plan put forward by the US-led Board of Peace to give up its weapons in exchange for an Israeli troop withdrawal. However, the Israeli government said the proposal was insufficient.

Breaking.title: Nepal PM Balendra Shah visit: India to give $1.62bn economic package
Breaking.text:
Nepal's Prime Minister Balen Shah has repeatedly called for his country to be treated as an equal by its powerful neighbours. His first visit to the Indian capital, Delhi, put that approach to the test, as both sides sought to reset a relationship strained by years of friction.

The contrast between the two leaders was striking.

Shah, 36, wearing his trademark black suit and sunglasses, stood beside Prime Minister Narendra Modi, 76, dressed in white. Shah rose to power after a wave of Gen Z-led protests toppled his predecessor.

Modi, meanwhile, is serving a third term and has recently faced student-led protests in India.

Yet, the two leaders seemed determined to project warmer relations. They exchanged gifts, inspected a military guard of honour and jointly flagged off a new cross-border train service.

For Nepal, the stakes were about far more than repairing diplomatic ties.

The two countries announced a series of agreements covering trade, hydropower, transport and education for Nepali youths.

India, more crucially, unveiled a $1.6bn (£1.22bn) support package as Nepal recovers from devastating floods earlier this year.

The floods killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands still missing. Shah's government has faced criticism over support for families which lost homes and loved ones.

The country faces a huge reconstruction challenge. The government estimates rebuilding could cost as much as $4.8bn. Addressing the UN General Assembly in September, Shah warned that when climate disasters devastate poorer countries, "the answer cannot simply be another mega-loan".

Modi pledged nearly $1.6bn in Indian support. Most of it will come as a line of credit for energy projects, alongside about $400m in grants for reconstruction and infrastructure.

While Nepal would have preferred a larger package, former senior Nepali diplomat Vijay Kant Karna says it is still "a significant amount" and could help stabilise a relationship that has often been uneasy.

A Hindu-majority nation wedged between India and China, Nepal has long had to navigate competing interests from its two giant neighbours. Allegations of political interference and an unresolved border dispute have frequently complicated ties with India.

Nepal's former Prime Minister, KP Sharma Oli, who leads a communist party, was widely viewed as being closer to China. Shah, by contrast, emerged as a political outsider when he was elected earlier this year. The former rapper, then 35, led a party that was only four years old.

His new approach of dealing with India may explain why the border dispute was largely absent from the leaders' public remarks, although the joint statement acknowledged that outstanding issues remained.

According to Govind Pokharel, a former vice-chairman of Nepal's National Planning Commission, Shah's government may have chosen to set contentious issues aside in order to secure progress on more immediate development needs.

"Right now you can go home and convince the young Nepalis that it will be handled later," Pokhrel says, "but if they don't deal with these issues in the future, there will be criticism."

Veteran Indian diplomat Anil Trigunayat says both sides appear to have opted to leave the dispute to established mechanisms rather than engage in what he calls "cartographic aggressions".

There were other gains for Nepal as a result of the Delhi visit.

As a landlocked country heavily dependent on India for trade, Nepal secured access to two additional Indian ports, Kandla and Paradip. The two sides also agreed to improve road and rail connectivity.

The leaders jointly inaugurated a train service linking Ayodhya in India, revered by Hindus as the birthplace of Lord Ram, with Janakpur in Nepal, traditionally regarded as the birthplace of his wife Sita.

There was, however, disappointment on aviation.

Nepal has long sought greater access to Indian airspace in order to attract international traffic to its airports at Bhairahawa and Pokhara.

Some analysts believe the lack of an agreement reflects Indian concerns over Chinese involvement in the two airport projects.

"The airport in Pokhara can pose certain security challenges for India, so it is a more complicated issue to resolve," says Trigunayat.

India did, however, agree to make an existing air route linking Kathmandu, Bhairahawa and Lucknow bidirectional.

"Nepal invested a huge amount of money in those airports," says Pokharel. "It fell short of expectations, but the bidirectional route is a breakthrough."

Shah must now manage relations with China as he seeks to balance the interests of Nepal's two much larger neighbours.

For now he returns home with substantial financial commitments from India as Nepal continues the long task of rebuilding.

Breaking.title: Nigeria boat accident: At least 29 dead after overcrowded boat capsizes in Bayelsa
Breaking.text:
Nigerian search and rescue teams are racing against time to find survivors after a boat carrying mourners travelling to a funeral capsized on Friday.

Twenty-nine bodies have been recovered and 50 people rescued so far, a spokesperson for the National Emergency Management Agency (Nema) told the BBC.

The government has responded by ordering stricter enforcement of safety standards on the country's inland waterways.

Overcrowding, poor maintenance and failure to observe safety regulations have contributed to previous deadly accidents on Nigeria's rivers.

The boat was travelling from Ayama community when it developed mechanical problems, according to police spokesperson Musa Mohammed.

Passengers asked the boat operator to steer towards land, but he allegedly declined, leading to the accident.

Survivors have described the panic that followed as passengers struggled to swim and stay afloat while waiting for emergency rescue services.

"As I swam, people were dragging me to the bottom, and I bit one woman and saved myself," Charity Ebikaboaere told local media outlet Arise News.

"Our things, our money, phones, everything lost, but me and my siblings are alive," said another survivor, Tari Samuel.

Nema spokesman Manzo Ezekiel raised concerns about the use of untrained boat operators and passengers travelling without life jackets.

"Some of them believe they're from river areas and they know how to swim," he said, warning that familiarity with waterways should not replace basic safety precautions.

There have been reports that the boat was carrying more than 300 people but the Nema spokesperson said this wasn't correct. He did not say how many people were on board but said it was overcrowded.

The accident happened in a region where waterways are a key means of transport, especially for communities with limited road access.

"Overloading, speeding, recklessness and traveling without life jackets must stop. No journey is worth a life," Bayelsa Commissioner for Information Ebiuwou Koku-Obiyai said in a statement on Saturday.

Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has relayed his condolences to the victims' families.

In a statement posted on X, Tinubu said he had directed relevant federal disaster response agencies to work together to ensure a successful rescue and recovery operation.

He also ordered that his election rally on Saturday, in Ibadan, Oyo State, be held without much fanfare in honour of those who lost their lives.

Boat accidents are a recurring problem in Nigeria, particularly in riverine communities where boats are a major means of transport.

In August, at least 50 people, mostly children, died after an overloaded boat capsized in the north-western Sokoto state. In January, at least 25 people died when a leaking boat capsized in Yobe state, in the north-east.

Business.title: Why Jensen Huang proved too big to fire
Business.text:
There have been three jaw-dropping moments in the past few hours around Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia chief executive after he admitted an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy.

The shock announcement of his return to the chipmaker was followed by the addition of one trillion dollars of stock market value to Nvidia.

Then it was the moment President Trump admitted the obvious: that it was his "You're unfired" message direct to the board that changed the decision.

The nature of the U-turn is clear from what Nvidia was saying just last week. The board was clear that Huang was not returning.

The interim management had also suggested some shifts in strategy away from the Huang era.

All of that is now in the dustbin of corporate history.

This is a comeback that exceeds the return of Sam Altman to OpenAI or Steve Jobs to Apple, in terms of sheer numbers.

The reason for the turnaround was pretty clear in the first statement. The US government had said there were no national security concerns with his reinstatement. Such a reassurance could only have come from the White House.

And an hour later President Trump revealed that he had spoken directly to the Nvidia board.

This is where I go back to my own conversation with Jensen Huang last September, where he openly advocated for allowing Chinese access to advanced Nvidia microchips. He was one of the few people in the world who could credibly say he knew the minds of both President Trump and President Xi.

Reports in the US say there were splits in the Trump administration between China hawks wanting to restrict exports, and others who backed Huang's argument.

There is still an independent investigation into the company's compliance with export controls.

Nvidia's chips are critical to the development of frontier artificial intelligence systems. Jensen Huang's influence over this pipeline meant he was more important than many world leaders.

This is a move of importance not just to the flagging US tech stock boom, but the future of the world economy, of US politics, and of course the geopolitical race between the US and China.

The recent doubts about Nvidia struck at the heart of the AI boom. This is after all a company actually generating phenomenal amounts of real sales - over $400bn (£305bn) this year, compared with $27bn four years ago.

Nvidia's stock market valuation has been used as a critical form of financing for other companies to construct data centres.

A complex web of loans, guarantees, and shareholdings helped spread and sustain the AI boom. Jensen Huang's exit had raised doubts about the fragility of this system, and the interim management had suggested a more "disciplined and selective" approach.

The concerns about so-called "circular financing" still raise concerns from some analysts. The public backlash against datacentres and AI evident at the US midterm elections also point to a changed environment.

The Democrats in Congress have vowed to investigate both the President and Mr Huang, and he is due to appear before them next week. Jensen Huang is at the centre of it all - the technology, the financing, the US politics and the geopolitics.

Today has proven Jensen Huang was in fact, too big to fire.

Business.title: Nvidia value climbs by almost $1tn and tech stocks rally after Jensen Huang returns
Business.text:
Nvidia's market value rose by nearly $1 trillion as its share price skyrocketed after the tech firm reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive with immediate effect.

His shock reinstatement comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned after admitting an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy, a period in which shares in the chipmaker have also fallen significantly.

Nvidia shares rose by more than 31% which also lifted stock markets, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq climbing by 6.5% and the S&P 500 also rose 4.75%.

Tech stocks more broadly have also rallied following large falls on Friday, with much of the rally starting in pre-market trading before Huang's return was announced.

Other chipmakers experienced large increases following Monday's announcement from the Nvidia board. Shares in Micron Technology jumped 19%, while AMD shares rose nearly 7%.

Tesla shares also lept up by nearly 11.5%, while other tech gains were more muted by comparison: Amazon shares were up nearly 3.5%, and Apple and Microsoft rose by less than 2%.

While the surge in Nvidia shares was large and drove its market value back towards $4tn, the firm's share price remains about 21% down from a month ago.

A sharp drop occurred on 4 November, after the Democrat's midterm election victory sparked fears of tougher AI regulation to come led to a broad tech stock sell-off.

On Friday alone, Nvidia shares fell by 13.7% as tech stocks more broadly fell, and as Reuters reported - unconfirmed by the BBC - that the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) over its accounting practices.

Nvidia is a key firm at the core of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, with the chips it makes central to the industry.

Nvidia's board of directors voted unanimously to reinstate the firm's co-founder following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him, the company said - but US President Donald Trump has claimed he "convinced" the board to reinstate Huang.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at brokerage firm XTB, said Huang's return showed Huang was the "godfather" of AI, and "has a talismanic influence over the sector".

"Barely two weeks ago this man was ousted from the company that he founded due to serious misconduct and potential national security issues," she said.

"Even though Huang did not hold special voting shares on the board, Nvidia's directors cannot see a future for the company without him."

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said Huang's reinstatement was an astonishing about-turn for Nvidia, particularly given reports of an as-yet unconfirmed SEC investigation.

"This is the biggest corporate U-turn in living memory. To go from being embroiled in a spy scandal to being reinstated as the head of one of the world's most valuable companies in less than a fortnight is nothing short of remarkable," he said.

"Today's stock market rebound represents a massive sigh of relief by investors. However, one cannot rule out a more conservative approach by Huang going forward.

"His every move will be scrutinised by the market, and he may wish to tread more carefully to protect his integrity and ensure that Nvidia is being run responsibly."

Politicians are also demanding greater scrutiny.

Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said Huang's reinstatement "reportedly at the encouragement of Trump Administration officials and without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation."

She added: "What is abundantly clear is that the AI industry requires guardrails and oversight."

Business.title: Capita shares plunge 70% as boss quits after civil service pensions failure
Business.text:
Shares in outsourcing business Capita have sunk 70% after its boss stepped down as the saga over public sector pensions drags on.

Chief executive Adolfo Hernandez has agreed with the firm's board to leave with "immediate effect", admitting that the company had "not delivered" for members of the UK's Civil Service pension scheme.

The scheme, which manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK, has been mired in controversy, with tens of thousands of retiring civil servants having faced delays receiving their pension payments.

Capita has cut its profit forecast, partly due to the problems surrounding the scheme, and says it plans to raise £190m to bolster its finances.

Capita took over the administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme in December last year.

One Cabinet Office minister last month labelled the company's progress in improving how it runs the scheme as "abysmal".

Hernandez, who will be replaced by current chief financial officer Pablo Andres, said: "I am proud of the groundwork we have laid and the progress we have made under my leadership.

"Of course, within that I recognise that we have not delivered the service that members of the Civil Service pension scheme deserve."

Capita said it was now expecting its underlying operating profit for 2027 to be hit by between £85m and £95m, having previously expected a reduction of up to £40m.

This comes from the extra cost of the recovery plan, as well the loss of two other "major" contracts in the defence and pension solutions divisions.

Capita said it was planning an equity raise of £190m in the first half of next year, in order for the company to "move forward from a more stable foundation".

The backlog of payments from the civil service pension scheme has been described as "hell" by people who have failed to receive money, some of whom retired early owing to ill health.

BBC Radio 4's Money Box programme has been hearing from people caught up in the saga, and left in financial hardship.

Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs the Public Accounts Committee of MPs, said: "The mishandling of the civil service pension scheme has caused severe hardship for some scheme members, particularly considerably delayed bereavement payments.

"The PAC will continue to pursue this dreadful matter and we can only hope that the new acting Chief Executive, Pablo Andres, will be able to get a grip on this whole affair."

Business.title: Catering giant Compass Group to shift main stock market listing to US in further blow to UK
Business.text:
Catering giant Compass Group is planning to switch its primary stock market listing from the UK to the US in a move which will deal another blow to the London Stock Exchange.

A source close to the company told the BBC an official announcement was expected to be made in its full-year results on Tuesday.

Compass Group is made up of several brands which supply food and drink to various places, ranging from football stadiums and visitor attractions to schools, universities and large corporations.

It is understood the proposed shift to the US, which was first reported by the Financial Times, external, is being made due to the number of investors and the increasing business Compass has across the Atlantic.

North America accounts for two-thirds of its business, which drove its total 2025 revenues to $46.1bn.

However, such a move would deal a further blow to the London Stock Exchange (LSE), which has seen a growing number of firms leave the UK to list shares in the US in recent years.

These include tech firm Arm Holdings, Just Eat, Deliveroo and Paddy Power's parent company Flutter.

Long-running speculation also remains over the future of London stalwarts Shell and pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca, which began listing shares in New York in February.

Compass describes itself as "possibly the biggest business you've never heard of" due to its plethora of catering and hospitality brands it operates its business under, which include Levy, Bon Appétit, Eurest, Morrison Healthcare and Chartwells.

Business.title: Energy bills will soar - here's how you can ease the pain
Business.text:
Energy prices are forecast to rise by 26% for millions of homes in January, but experts say there are ways to keep a check on rising bills.

Here are four areas to consider ahead of the increase.

Energy regulator Ofgem's price cap, as well as suppliers' fixed deals, set a limit on the price of each unit of energy, not the total bill.

So, you pay for what you use. Millions of people have cut back on their energy consumption during years of relatively high prices.

With the unit price of gas, in particular, set to soar, experts say you should take a fresh look at your energy use and renew good habits.

Research foundation Nesta suggests:

turning down the flow temperature on a combi boiler - usually indicated by a radiator icon, to make it operate more efficiently

turning off the pre-heat facility on some combi boilers, which would have kept some water heated up when not in use

turning down the thermostat one degree, although 18C is the recommended minimum

closing all curtains at night

lowering radiator valves outside of the living room

turning off the heating before April

These are small changes but - alongside washing clothes at 30C, blocking draughts and batch cooking - they can reduce energy use and bills.

Ofgem says about five million people still pay their bill when it arrives every three months, rather than receive a monthly bill often initially based on an estimate.

Taking regular meter readings, or having a smart meter, while paying by monthly direct debit solves that problem.

Paying by direct debit costs significantly less than by so-called standard credit - typically £138 cheaper a year.

Customers on prepayment schemes - usually people on low incomes struggling to pay bills - used to pay a higher rate than others, but now they pay slightly less than the capped direct debit variable rate.

Various deals may rely on paying by direct debit or having a smart meter.

Moving to a fixed energy tariff means the price you are charged per unit of gas or electricity does not change every three months, although the total bill will still vary depending on how much energy you use.

The trouble is that it is very difficult to work out whether a fixed deal is a good deal at the moment, for those renewing fixed deals or looking for one for the first time.

Some fixed deals are available at unit prices below the next forecast price cap level. But should energy prices fall sharply then a longer-term fix might not seem such good value compared with the price cap.

So consumer group Which? also recommends paying close attention to any exit fees when picking a fixed deal. If variable prices fall below your fixed rate and you want to get out of it before the end of your agreement period, you may have to pay a hefty sum.

Before you fix, consumer website MoneySavingExpert advises you look at all the deals available, not just what your own supplier is offering.

The government will give a £100 payment to millions of homes to help cover winter energy costs. It will go to homes in council tax bands A to D in England, with the equivalent expected in Scotland and Wales.

There are also a range of other forms of support specifically for people on low incomes.

This winter anyone on means-tested benefits will get £150 off their electricity bill.

Your supplier will apply the discount automatically unless you are in Scotland, where you will need to contact your energy company to ask for the help.

Some people will also be eligible for a Cold Weather Payment, external and most pensioners will receive the winter fuel payment.

Beyond that, most energy suppliers offer hardship grants for people struggling to pay their bills and the government's Fuel Direct Scheme, external can help you repay energy debt.

You can get more advice from Ofgem, external, Citizens Advice, external, or your own energy supplier. Trade body Energy UK has a list of support schemes, external.

People on low incomes may also be eligible for grants to help with insulating their homes, and there are local schemes offering grants for solar panels, heat pumps and the like.

But if you are hunting around for grants, watch out for scams pretending to be official money-off schemes.

Business.title: Poundland is facing collapse - what's gone wrong?
Business.text:
The future of Poundland hangs in the balance as it faces a possible collapse into administration.

Its owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, put it up for sale in September, but then rejected offers to keep the business afloat.

Poundland has a major presence on the High Street, with 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades under the Dealz brand.

If it were to collapse, the jobs of its 11,000 employees would be at risk, as well as potentially thousands of others at firms that supply the retailer.

How have we got here?

People have not stopped shopping at Poundland - quite the opposite.

Although the chain was struggling when it was sold by Pepco last year for £1, the business turned a corner over the year to September, going from a £68m loss to an £18.1m profit before interest, tax and certain accounting charges.

Going into the vital Christmas period, first-quarter like-for-like sales were up 7% and operational profits of £1.9m were up £1.2m on last year.

Halloween sales were 11.4% higher than last year - this is usually a good indicator of how a retailer will do at Christmas, says retail analyst Catherine Shuttleworth of Savvy Marketing.

According to Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency specialist Begbies Traynor: "This isn't a story about shoppers abandoning Poundland. The tills are busier than they were a year ago."

She adds: "On the face of it, a turnaround seems well under way."

However, Gordon Brothers has been restricting Poundland's access to cash needed to restock stores and meet day-to-day expenses.

It had frozen about £50m in funds leading to concerns Poundland's shops would run out of stock.

Gordon Brothers released around £21m over two weeks recently, giving the chain a little more breathing space.

Poundland seems to be facing "a funding and ownership problem rather than a trading collapse", Palmer says.

However, while Poundland boss Barry Williams says the business is making a "strong recovery", Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".

It says it has provided significant funding to support the company's ability to trade since it acquired the business.

It has also made about £18m from a combination of debt interest payments and other fees and charges.

As well as being Poundland's owner, it is one of its lenders, and is owed loans, including a £22.5m shareholder loan it inherited when it bought the business for £1.

As the main creditor, Gordon Brothers would be first in line to get paid back if the business goes under - but its suppliers are not.

"When the owner is also the main lender, its first priority is recovering [loans]," says Palmer. "Sometimes the route that best protects the lender is different from the one that saves the most jobs, and that tension is why this has become such a political story."

Irish firm Martin Property Group has offered to buy the business as a going concern, while London-based holding company Xyra Group has also made a rescue bid, although doubts remain about the credibility of Xyra's offer.

A German investment firm, Zachert Private Equity, is also understood to have made a late offer.

Gordon Brothers has also been weighing options to break Poundland up.

The US company's view is that ultimately breaking the retailer up will provide more security for employees in the long term, because any buyers of its store estate will also have to agree to keep the employees on.

Insiders who are critical of how Gordon Brothers has handled the Poundland sale say it is driving the business into the ground to make money through the insolvency process.

But the investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claim.

For now, Poundland has avoided immediate collapse after a deadline was extended by 10 days to find a rescue deal.

Shuttleworth says the future of Poundland is "really unclear, with the owners and the management at loggerheads about its future".

Palmer says there are two ways forward for Poundland - either a solvent deal, where the company gets bought and carries on trading, or a collapse followed by a break-up.

"The immediate make-or-break issue is Christmas: a value retailer that can't get stock on its shelves in November and December is in serious trouble, whatever its full-year results say," says Palmer.

There has been political pressure on Gordon Brothers from both Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds. They have called for answers over why the Martin Property Group offer to buy the business, which would have protected jobs, was rejected.

A committee of MPs also questioned Gordon Brothers last week, adding to pressure.

But Shuttleworth says that as a US firm Gordon Brothers appears "unmoved" by the arguments that the UK government has put forward.

Business.title: Pip assessments need 'fundamental overhaul', report to say
Business.text:
A review into the personal independence payment (Pip) will call for a "fundamental overhaul" of the assessment process to "better recognise people's varying costs and needs", the disability minister has said.

Sir Stephen Timms has been looking into disability benefits in England and Wales for the past year and found the set up was "no longer fit for purpose".

Writing in the Times, external, he said his review, to be published on Tuesday, would recommend people with the most severe conditions have a "fast track" process which is "less burdensome".

It comes after a separate review into young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) recommended Pip be scrapped and replaced for under-25s.

Sir Stephen, who produced his report alongside disability groups, carers, clinicians and MPs, said that while Pip had the "right aims" when it was created, there have been "marked shifts in the nature of disability and ill health" in the 13 years since.

He said there had been "substantial growth in claims for mental health and neurodiverse conditions as well as changes to wider society and the workplace".

"For those with the most severe conditions and end of life care, the review recommends a fast track which is less burdensome, with assessment capacity freed up for other cases.

"Where claimants do not have additional costs or care needs, we should be signposting them to services and support."

He added: "Someone with a lifelong or degenerative illness should not need regular reassessments which feel adversarial and unnecessary.

"Disabled people must have the chance to participate fully in everyday life, including in work, and need a more personalised, flexible system that supports them to do so, rather than itself being a barrier."

The Timms review was commissioned after a U-turn from former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's government on a plan for major benefit reform, which attempted to reduce the welfare bill by £5bn a year.

More than 130 MPs, including 120 from Labour, signed an amendment to reject plans to cut disability and sickness-related benefit payments in 2025.

The rebels said they opposed the plans because of the number of people expected to be pushed into relative poverty and a lack of consultation at the time.

Sir Stephen's long-awaited review comes only a week after a former Labour Health Secretary Alan Milburn handed down his proposed reforms to tackle youth unemployment.

The government welcomed the Milburn review, which included a recommendation to move those aged 18 to 24 off Pip and the health element of universal credit, and onto an entirely new benefits system.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he thought the "same philosophy" could be applied "right through the age range".

At this stage it is unclear how both of the reviews will complement one another.

No 10 has said the government would consider the Timms review "alongside Milburn's and respond in the coming weeks".

Downing Street has not ruled out the possibility that some people who currently receive Pip could have a reduced entitlement in the future and would not say if the review's recommendations would lead to a reduced welfare bill.

The cost of Pip is expected to rise to more than £41bn by 2030, up from £15bn in 2020. It was being claimed by 4m people in the UK as of 30 April 2026, according to the Department for Work and Pensions.

Though reforming the benefit has frequently been looked at as a way to reduce the Treasury's welfare bill, disability charities have described it as a lifeline for many.

Ahead of the Timms review being handed down, disability equality charity Scope said ministers must ensure Pip is not weakened.

"Life costs more when you're disabled, whether you work or not," executive director James Taylor said, adding that Pip was "vital financial support".

"We know there is real fear among disabled people that changes could leave them unable to afford the essentials."

The disability benefit system is devolved in Scotland and will not change in line with England and Wales; however the Timms Review could impact the funding the Scottish government receives.

Disability benefits are also devolved in Northern Ireland, but in practice it reflects any changes made to the system in England and Wales.

Business.title: South East Water reports loss after penalties and supply failures
Business.text:
South East Water has reported a half-year loss after penalties and £29m of costs following disruption to water supplies over the summer.

The company, which serves about 2.4 million customers across south-east England, recorded a pre-tax loss of £22.9m in the six months to 30 September, compared with a profit of £18.2m during the same period last year.

In July, regulator Ofwat ordered the company to spend £30.5m on improvements after supply interruptions hit customers across Kent and Sussex which affected more than 286,000 customers.

The company spent £29m responding to further supply interruptions during summer heatwaves in Kent and Sussex.

This included providing bottled water, setting up emergency water stations and compensating customers.

South East Water said it had set aside £14.6m in its latest financial results to cover the redress package.

The company supplies water to customers in Kent, East and West Sussex, Surrey, Hampshire and Berkshire.

Hosepipe bans remain in force across all areas supplied by South East Water.

Business.title: Anthropic may have solved major maths problem Reimann hypothesis
Business.text:
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.

Levent Alpöge said, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.

If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".

The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.

As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.

It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.

Named after the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.

Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.

Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.

"The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."

"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.

The complete textual proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.

Terence Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday, external that digestion of the proof - the process of understanding the reasoning behind it and how it connects to other mathematical ideas - is still some way off.

"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.

No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.

OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.

More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.

The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.

Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external.

A group of maths scholars said, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".

"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.

A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.

It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.
